guest.bio_context: Mike Collison spent approximately a decade in the oil patch and has worked in the trades since his teenage years. He worked on the rigs in Alberta for several years, including extended hitches of up to 78 straight days and 46 consecutive night shifts. He is now in recovery and actively involved in a 12-step program, having transformed his relationship with substance use after a period of active addiction.

context.real_quote: Without the ability to look in a mirror and see those things reflected back at you, until you can find someone else to walk that walk with you, you cannot heal.
key_stats: Age 7 to 12: period of rape and abuse by a family friend and his son
2006: detoxed from heroin in Saskatoon after relocating from Victoria; was 21 years old
Nearly 3 weeks: duration of raw detoxification in corner of apartment
12 years: period of abstinence from chemical drugs after 2006, though continued drinking and smoking pot
2015: married; 2016: purchased house; 2017: son Easton born
78 straight days: longest hitch worked on the rigs
46 straight night shifts at 12 hours per day: longest continuous night shift period on rigs
2019: dog Ramsey died from aggressive cancer; triggered relapse into active addiction
December 2019: moment addiction shifted from recreational use to escape and numbing
March 2020: COVID-19 hit; left the rigs

pending_qa.q: What is the relationship between childhood abandonment of healthy relationships and adult patterns of seeking chaos and toxicity?
pending_qa.r: Mike describes how he had no frame of reference for healthy relationships because everything in his life was transactional—like an ATM interaction. When he was in a genuinely healthy and loving relationship 15 years ago, he destroyed it because it felt too vanilla and lacked passion; looking back, it was just normal. He felt comfortable in chaotic, toxic situations because they gave him something to manage and control, whereas genuine care and acceptance felt foreign and abnormal to him.

pending_qa.q: How does a person begin to recognize their own worth after years of believing they deserved mistreatment?
pending_qa.r: Mike reflects that the hardest part for him now is realizing he actually has worth. Looking back on his life choices and the dark moments, he wishes he could have seen it 20 years ago. He had to do a lot of work and talking about his trauma to sit across from someone like Trevor who simply created space without judgment, allowing him to feel that he didn't have to go through things alone. This experience of being accepted by another man safely was transformative in beginning to understand his own value.

pending_qa.q: What triggers prompt someone to return to substance use after claiming they have overcome addiction?
pending_qa.r: Mike describes the rationalization process: after 12 years sober from hard drugs, he convinced himself at a party that everyone else was doing it, so one use wouldn't hurt. He then announced to himself that he had clearly beaten addiction and was cured because he could use once without immediately relapsing. This false confidence lasted only briefly before he began dabbling back into use in 2018, eventually opening the doors to full-blown addiction again.
